text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- More young people are living off social welfare with nearly half of new applicants seeking benefits aged under 25, according to a new study by the Social Services.
- About 80 billion crowns was wiped off the value of Swedish shares on Tuesday when the Stockholm general index plunged about four percent, following a fall in New York over Easter.

- Prices of summer homes are on the rise with the biggest increase so far in the southern area of Skane. Last year a summer house cost on average 370,000 crowns while an average summer home in Stockholm cost 581,000 crowns, according to Statistics Sweden.
- Newspaper deliverers could be out on strike again on Thursday and Friday in a continuing dispute over wages.

- The Stockholm Stock Exchange dropped 4.34 percent on Tuesday, the largest plunge in one day since the volatile currency and bond autumn of 1992 when it dived five percent. Small investors could, however, benefit from staying calm and not selling shares in a panic as bourse jitters should wear off, analysts said.
- New rules for company cars have lifted Swedish car sales with registrations jumping 43 percent in March -- and April sales could be even stronger, according to industry figures.

- Local Social Democratic party leaders are worried about dwindling voter support for the minority Social Democratic government and the increased support for the conservative opposition, the Moderates, as shown by the most recent survey by pollster Sifo. The poll, published at the weekend, was the most extreme to date and showed the Social Democrats with only 27.6 percent of support and the Moderates with 34 percent.

- Swedish stocks plunged and interest rates climbed on Tuesday after the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled during the Easter holiday. The general index fell 4.72 percent in early trading. Analysts said stocks will continue to perform weakly until this summer but then will climb.

- Professor Lennart Sjoberg of the Stockholm School of Economics said developments on the Swedish stock market on Tuesday showed how psychological factors not only rational judgements sway shareholders. He said Swedes are easily frightened and quick to exit an unstable market.

- Swedish car makers Volvo AB and Saab both gained ground in March against their foreign competitors on their home market. Total new registrations for cars increased last month by 42 percent to 20,060, according to industry group Bilindustriforeningen, the Swedish Association of Automobile Manufacturers.

- Telecoms group Ericsson has signed two contracts in Brazil with a combined value of 1.15 billion crowns to expand mobile telephone networks in the states of Sao Paolo and Pernambuco. Ericsson chief executive Lars Ramqvist expects Brazil this year to become the company's third largest single market after the U.S. and Canada.
